title: Fire in Ḍombī's House
summary: Fire has caught in the house of Ḍombī, an outcaste woman, and the poet, taking the moon, sprinkles water; the fire shows no flame or smoke and climbs Meru's peak into the sky, Hari, Hara and Brahmā burst, the nine qualities and the teaching fall, and at the end water rises through five channels. Munidatta reads the fire as the fire of the passion of great bliss, Caṇḍālī blazing at the navel, Ḍombī as the purified avadhūtī, the moon as conventional bodhicitta that puts the fire out, and the three gods as channels of the body that the fire burns (cp.47.m2–m5). His Sanskrit breaks off in the last couplet, and the Tibetan translation's continuation of the comment (cp.47.m7) speaks there of bodhicitta going back up by the path of the avadhūtī.

lines.translit: /du dz+dza ra zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs chos pa'i zhabs kyi'o/
lines.gloss: du dz+dza ra (name of the melody; taken as Guñjarī) · called (zhes bya ba'i) · melody (glu dbyangs) · of Dharma (chos pa'i) · venerable, -pāda (zhabs) · belonging to (kyi'o)

flags.note: Translated from the Tibetan (Toh 2293): the Bengali edition has no rāga line for this song. Before the song the Nepal manuscript writes guñjarīpādānāṃ, 'of Guñjarīpāda', where a poet's name usually stands; it is not verse and has been emended out of 1a. The Tibetan du dz+dza ra is taken as a garbled Guñjarī (the Tibetan of song 5 has gu dz+dza rI), which the manuscript's guñjarī- supports. The Tibetan names the poet chos pa'i zhabs, 'Dharmapāda'; rendered Dhāmapāda after the signature (5a, dhāma) and Munidatta's dhāmapāda (cp.47.m1).

lines.gloss: lotus · vajra (kuliśa) · in the middle of (loc.) · become? (bha-i-ma; reading unclear) · joined, met (fem. past?)
lines.en: Joined in the middle of [lotus]{lotus} and [vajra]{vajra},

flags.note: bhaima mialī is unclear. I take bha-i-ma as bhaïa, 'having become', and mialī as a feminine past form of mil-, 'join, meet' (compare lāgeli, fem., in 2a), agreeing with Caṇḍālī in 1b: 'Joined … Caṇḍālī blazed'. Alternatives: (a) a first person, 'I was joined', which Munidatta's mama, 'for me', in his paraphrase might reflect (cp.47.m2); (b) a noun, 'union came about'. The Tibetan has gyur pa blangs, 'took what had come to be', as if mialī meant 'taken'. I chose the participle because it uses the Bengali agreement and adds no subject.
The Tibetan line has the usual Tibetan order, vajra before lotus (rdo rje pad+ma'i dbus su, 'in the middle of vajra and lotus'); the Bengali puts the lotus first.

lines.gloss: sameness · by yoga, by joining (instr.) · blazed, kindled · Caṇḍālī · (dhru: cue to sing the refrain; not translated)

flags.note: joem̐ is the instrumental of joa (yoga): 'by yoga' or 'by joining'. The Tibetan has mnyam nyid sbyor bas, 'by joining in sameness'. Rendered 'through the yoga of sameness'; 'by union with sameness' is the alternative.
Shastri prints ধ্রু after 1b, before the refrain. Munidatta names couplet 2 as the refrain (dhruvapada, cp.47.m3), so the cue here looks misplaced. Not translated.

lines.gloss: burning (dāha) · Ḍombī · in the house (loc.) · caught, took hold (fem. past) · fire

flags.note: ḍāha, 'burning', stands first. Munidatta joins it to the fire, 'the fire joined with the burning of the passion of great bliss' (cp.47.m3), as rendered here; it could also be an exclamation, 'Burning!'. The Tibetan line has the house itself burnt by the fire and blazing (khang pa me yis tshig nas 'bar).

lines.translit: saha ṣali lai ṣiñca hūm̐ pāṇī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: saha (? 'with') · ṣali (?) [saha ṣali taken as 'moon', after Munidatta's sasahara] · taking · sprinkle (siñc-) · I · water · (dhru)

flags.note: saha ṣali, as printed, does not mean 'moon' (saha is 'with'; ṣali is unexplained). The moon rests only on Munidatta's citation of the word as sasaharam (śaśadhara, 'hare-bearer', the moon; cp.47.m3) and on the Tibetan ri bong 'dzin pa'i chu, 'the hare-holder's water'. The print may be a corruption of sasahara. I kept 'moon' in the line; the alternative is to mark the two words as untranslated.

হূঁ is the pronoun 'I' (Old Bengali hāũ), not the seed syllable hūṃ; Munidatta's first person ('I put out that fire', nirvāpaṇaṃ karomi, cp.47.m3) agrees. The Tibetan reads an imperative instead: ri bong 'dzin pa'i chu ni long la gtor bar gyis, 'take the moon's water and sprinkle it!' (long perhaps for longs, 'take'), and joins the moon to the water where the Bengali has two objects.

lines.translit: nau khara jālā dhuma na diśai
lines.gloss: not (na u?) · fierce (khara; Tib. 'grass') · flame, blaze (jvālā) · smoke · not · is seen
lines.en: No fierce flame, no [smoke]{smoke} is seen;

flags.note: nau khara jālā: I take nau as na u, 'not', khara as 'fierce, sharp' and jālā as 'flame' (jvālā), following Munidatta, who sets outer fire, whose fierce blaze (tīvraṃ jvalana) and smoke are seen, against the fire of knowledge, which is not (cp.47.m4). The Tibetan reads khara as grass or straw (rtswa ni 'bar ba ma yin, 'the grass does not blaze'; compare Bengali khaṛ, 'straw'). nau could also be 'nine' or 'new', but neither witness reads it so.

lines.translit: meru śikhara lai gaaṇa paisai || dhru ||
lines.gloss: Meru · peak · taking (or 'up to') · sky · enters · (dhru)

flags.note: lai, 'taking', as in 2b; here it may rather mean 'up to, by way of'. Munidatta has the fire absorbed 'at the tip of Sumeru's peak' (cp.47.m4); the Tibetan has it 'taken up onto Sumeru' (ri rab steng du blangs nas). The subject is unexpressed; 'it' (the fire, as Munidatta has it) is supplied.
The Bengali says Meru; the glossary's English for pl-sumeru is Sumeru, so Sumeru is used (see questions).

lines.gloss: bursts (Munidatta cites dāṭai, 'burns') · Hari and Hara · Brahmā (or 'brahmin') · full, all (?)
lines.en: [Hari, Hara and Brahmā]{p-hari-hara-brahma}, all of them, burst;

flags.note: Shastri prints ফাটই, 'bursts', and the line is translated so. Munidatta cites the verb as dāṭai and says the three are burned (etā dagdhā, cp.47.m5); the Tibetan line has tshig, 'burn'. Both witnesses point to dāṭai, 'burns', which would tie the gods to the fire of the refrain.

bāhma is taken as Brahmā, with Munidatta (vāhma, cp.47.m5) and the Tibetan (tshangs pa); the same spelling means 'brahmin' in song 10. bharā is unclear: 'full, all of them' (compare Bengali bharā, 'full') is assumed. The Tibetan's rje btsun, 'venerable lords', with plural rnams, might reflect a reading like bhaṭṭāra(ka), 'lord'; that is a guess.

lines.translit: phīṭā hai ṇabaguṇa śāsana paṛā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: wiped out, destroyed (?) · becomes · nine qualities, or nine-stranded · teaching, rule (śāsana) · fallen · (dhru)
lines.en: the [nine qualities]{navaguna} are wiped out, the [teaching]{sasana} has fallen.

flags.note: phīṭā hai is uncertain: taken as 'is wiped out, destroyed', perhaps chiming with phāṭai in 4a; paṛā as 'fallen'. ṇabaguṇa is 'nine qualities' (glossary); guṇa is also 'strand', so 'nine-stranded', the brahmin's sacred thread, is possible and would suit a couplet that names Hari, Hara and Brahmā. śāsana is 'teaching' (glossary); it can also be a rule or edict, or a settlement granted by royal charter.

The Tibetan line reads 'the nine qualities and the towns of the land also burn' (yon tan dgu dang yul gyi grong khyer rnams kyang tshig): towns where the Bengali has śāsana, and 'burn' again for the verb. Munidatta glosses navaguṇa as the nine winds and śāsana as the objects of the eye and the other senses (cp.47.m5).

lines.gloss: says · Dhāma · clearly, plainly (sphuṭa) · taking from the guru? (le + gure?; obscure) · know (or 'having known')
lines.en: [Dhāma]{p-dharma} says: taking it from the [guru]{guru}, know it plainly —

flags.note: leṅgūre is obscure. I divide it le + gure, 'taking … at (from) the guru', because the Tibetan line has blangs, 'taken' (gsal por blangs nas rab tu shes, 'clearly taking, know fully'), and Munidatta's paraphrase of this line brings in the glorious guru's feet (śrīgurucaraṇopāyena, cp.47.m6). He does not cite the word, so the division is a conjecture; lāṅgūla, 'tail', or another word is possible. Fallback: 'taking it, know it plainly', with the Tibetan, and the guru only in a note.

jāṇī is read as an imperative, 'know', as the Tibetan continuation of the comment has it ('know innate joy!', shes par gyis shig, cp.47.m7), where Munidatta has the poet address one who has not understood the path (cp.47.m6). It may instead be an absolutive: 'Dhāma says, having known it plainly…'.
The Tibetan reads the name as Dharma (d+harmas smras pa, 'Dharma says'); see the note at the head.

lines.gloss: through (in) the five channels (instr.-loc.) · rising · went · water · (dhru)
lines.en: through the [five channels]{pancanala} the [water]{water} has risen.

flags.note: uṭhe gela, 'rose and went', a compound verb: 'has risen, has gone up'. pañcanālem̐ is instrumental-locative, 'through' or 'in' five pipes or channels (nāla, 'tube, hollow stalk'); the Tibetan has rtsa phran lnga las, 'from the five minor channels', the subtle body's word.
Munidatta's Sanskrit breaks off before this line; the only comment on it is the Tibetan translation's continuation (cp.47.m7).

notes.text: The Bengali edition has no rāga line for this song, so the heading is translated from the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): du dz+dza ra zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs chos pa'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody called du dz+dza ra, of Chos pa'i zhabs'. du dz+dza ra is taken as a garbled Guñjarī, the rāga the Tibetan of song 5 transcribes gu dz+dza rI. In the Nepal manuscript, guñjarīpādānāṃ, 'of Guñjarīpāda', stands before the song where the poet's name usually stands; it is not part of the verse and has been removed from 1a. It looks like the rāga's name taken for a poet's. The poet names himself Dhāma (5a), and Munidatta calls him the siddha master Dhāmapāda (cp.47.m1); the Tibetan has chos pa'i zhabs, 'Dharmapāda', in its heading and comment, and d+harma in 5a.
rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung. The Tibetan has glu dbyangs, 'melody'.

Munidatta introduces the song as the siddha master Dhāmapāda, his mind full of supreme compassion and loving-kindness, setting out 'that same meaning' (tam evārtham), the theme of the song before (cp.47.m1). The Tibetan has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', instead.
vajra: the thunderbolt-diamond, emblem of the indestructible in tantric Buddhism. The song's word is kuliśa, a synonym; the songs often pair it with the lotus, as here.

Caṇḍālī: a woman of the Caṇḍāla community, which caste society ranked lowest and treated as untouchable. The yoginī tantras also give the name to a fire kindled at the navel; the Tibetan line has gtum mo, 'fierce woman', its word for that fire.

Munidatta paraphrases the couplet: through the sameness of wisdom and means (prajñopāyasamatā), and from the whirl of the wind of the passion of true, imperishable great bliss (an obscure compound), 'Caṇḍālī blazed for me at the navel, in the wheel of emanation' (cp.47.m2). The Tibetan comment agrees but has 'the fire of passion' ('dod chags kyi me) where the Sanskrit seems to have 'wind' (anila; perhaps read as anala, 'fire'), and 'the fire of gtum mo' for Caṇḍālī. The song names neither the navel nor the wheel.

The refrain is a house fire: the house of Ḍombī, a woman of the Ḍom caste, which caste society kept at the edge of town, catches fire, and the speaker sprinkles water, having taken the moon. In Indian poetry the moon is the cool one (śītāṃśu, 'cool-rayed') and a source of nectar, which may be why it serves against fire; that is my gloss, not the commentary's.

Munidatta says the refrain makes the same point plain. The fire is joined with the burning of the passion of great bliss; Ḍombī is the purified avadhūtī, in whose house it has caught; 'with that fire of the passion of great bliss I burned the support of the whole host of sense objects'. On the moon (sasaharam iti) he says: having taken, by the true guru's grace, conventional bodhicitta purified by vilakṣaṇa, I put out that fire. He adds the Dvikalpa (Hevajra) line on Caṇḍālī blazing at the navel (cp.47.m3). The Tibetan comment agrees, but has sbyong ba, 'purifying', perhaps for sbyor ba, 'attaching', where the Sanskrit has the fire 'caught' (lagna).

saha ṣali, as printed, does not plainly mean 'moon'. The rendering follows Munidatta, who cites the word as sasahara (śaśadhara, 'hare-bearer', a name of the moon; cp.47.m3), and the Tibetan line, which has ri bong 'dzin pa'i chu, 'the hare-holder's water'. হূঁ is the pronoun 'I', not the seed syllable hūṃ.

The Tibetan line turns the second half of the refrain into an instruction: 'take the moon's water and sprinkle it!' (ri bong 'dzin pa'i chu ni long la gtor bar gyis; long is perhaps for longs, 'take'). The Bengali has the speaker do it: 'I sprinkle'.

Munidatta says this verse, his second, states the nature of the fire of knowledge (jñānavahni). Outer fire is seen by its fierce blaze and smoke, but this fire is not seen; the negative is Shastri's suggestion in the comment ([na?]), and the Tibetan has it (ye shes kyi me ni mi mthong). Having burned being and nonbeing, it is absorbed at the tip of Sumeru's peak, in 'the sky', that is, in the wheel of great bliss (cp.47.m4). The song says only that no flame or smoke is seen and that it enters the sky.
Smoke is the stock sign from which Indian logic infers fire. A fire that shows no flame and no smoke is a paradox the line leaves standing.

The Tibetan line reads 'the grass does not blaze, no smoke is seen' (rtswa ni 'bar ba ma yin du ba mthong ba med), taking khara as straw or grass (compare Bengali khaṛ, 'straw'). Munidatta's 'fierce blaze' (tīvraṃ jvalana, cp.47.m4) takes it as 'fierce'.

Shastri prints phāṭai, 'bursts', and the line is translated so. Munidatta cites the verb as dāṭai and says the three are burned (dagdhā, cp.47.m5), and the Tibetan line has tshig, 'burn'; a reading dāṭai, 'burns', would tie the couplet to the fire of the refrain. Hari is Viṣṇu and Hara is Śiva; the Tibetan names them khyab 'jug and dbang phyug, with Brahmā (tshangs pa).

Munidatta reads couplet 4 in twilight language: bāhma (Brahmā) is the channel of excrement, Hari the channel of urine, Hara the channel of semen; these are burned, and above them lalanā, rasanā and the rest. Navaguṇa means the nine winds, and śāsana what is called the objects of the eye faculty and the other senses; having burned them, that same fire of passion itself becomes without intrinsic nature. He then cites Saraha (manamara…) (cp.47.m5). The Tibetan comment agrees on the three channels but has no nine winds: it explains 'the nine qualities and of the land' together as the eye faculty and the rest and what are called objects, and has these made without intrinsic nature by the fire of passion.
Munidatta introduces this couplet as his third verse (tṛtīyapadena); the Tibetan has rkang pa gnyis pas, 'with the second verse', apparently a slip (cp.47.m5).

The Tibetan line reads 'the nine qualities and the towns of the land also burn' (yon tan dgu dang yul gyi grong khyer rnams kyang tshig). Its towns stand where the Bengali has śāsana, a word that in eastern Indian usage can also mean a settlement granted by royal charter; whether the translators read it so is a guess.

The couplet names the three great gods of Brahmanical religion. If ṇabaguṇa is taken as 'nine-stranded', the brahmin's sacred thread, and śāsana as a brahmin teaching or charter, the whole couplet shows the Brahmanical order coming down in the fire. The thread reading is offered for the reviewer; the line follows the glossary's 'nine qualities'.

Munidatta says the fourth verse states the conviction (pratyayitā) of the fourth joy. Dhāmapāda says: 'O you who have not understood the path, by means of the glorious guru's feet, having rightly and clearly brought about the union of vajra and lotus…' (cp.47.m6). The Tibetan comment has 'as the condition (rkyen) of the fourth joy', rendering pratyaya literally.

Munidatta's Sanskrit stops in mid-sentence (sa), at the folio number [67]; a folio of the manuscript is missing here. Segment cp.47.m7 is the continuation in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), not Munidatta's Sanskrit: '…know innate joy. Its great bliss comes from the lotus: the bodhicitta that has reached the tip of the jewel, purified by the fourth joy, with nāda, to the lotus's nāda, as it says; that is, by the path of the avadhūtī it goes back again to that very place' (cp.47.m7). It is the only comment on 5b, and it does not gloss the water or the five channels explicitly.

leṅgūre is obscure; the rendering divides it le + gure, 'taking from the guru'. The Tibetan line has gsal por blangs nas rab tu shes, 'clearly taking, know fully', and Munidatta's paraphrase brings in the glorious guru's feet (cp.47.m6), but neither confirms the division.

pañcanāla: five pipes or channels (Sanskrit nāla, 'tube, hollow stalk'; compare Bengali nālā, 'drain'). The Tibetan line has rtsa phran lnga, 'five minor channels', its word for channels of the subtle body.

termsOmitted.reason: Tibetan only: the Tibetan line has yul gyi grong khyer, 'the towns of the land', where the Bengali reading text has śāsana, rendered 'teaching' (sasana). Discussed in a witness note.
Tibetan only: yul in yul gyi grong khyer, here 'land', not 'sense objects'; not in the Bengali reading text.

proposals.definition: A channel of the subtle body linked with excrement (Sanskrit viṭ, 'excrement', and nāḍikā, 'channel'; Tibetan dri chen gyi rtsa). Munidatta says that bāhma, Brahmā, in song 47 (4a) is twilight language for it, and names it with the channels of urine and semen as burned by the fire of passion (cp.47.m5).
proposals.rationale: Munidatta names three lower channels together in cp.47.m5. The glossary has the channel of semen (sukranadika) but not this one or the channel of urine, which the weave of this comment will need.

proposals.definition: A channel of the subtle body linked with urine (Sanskrit mūtra, 'urine', and nāḍī, 'channel'; Tibetan dri chu'i rtsa). Munidatta says that Hari in song 47 (4a) is to be understood as it, and names it with the channels of excrement and semen as burned by the fire of passion (cp.47.m5).
proposals.rationale: Companion to the channel of excrement and the existing channel of semen (sukranadika), all three named in cp.47.m5.

questions: Heading: the Bengali has no rāga line, so 'Rāga Guñjarī · Dhāmapāda' is translated from the Tibetan (du dz+dza ra, taken as a garbled Guñjarī; chos pa'i zhabs, 'Dharmapāda'). Is that acceptable, and should the heading or only the note mention the manuscript's guñjarīpādānāṃ?

1a: I read mialī as a feminine past participle agreeing with Caṇḍālī ('Joined in the middle of lotus and vajra, / … Caṇḍālī blazed'). Do you prefer a first person ('I was joined'), which Munidatta's mama might support, or 'union came about'?
2b: 'moon' rests only on Munidatta's sasahara and the Tibetan ri bong 'dzin pa; the printed saha ṣali does not mean 'moon'. Keep 'moon' in the line, as drafted, or mark the words as doubtful?
3b: the Bengali has Meru, but the glossary's English for pl-sumeru is Sumeru, which I used. Could 'Meru' be added as a variant so the line can follow the Bengali?
4a: translate the printed phāṭai, 'burst' (as drafted), or emend to dāṭai, 'burn', with Munidatta's citation and the Tibetan tshig?

4b: keep the glossary's 'nine qualities' for ṇabaguṇa, or prefer 'nine-stranded (thread)', the brahmin's sacred thread, which would make couplet 4 a picture of the Brahmanical order falling? And is 'wiped out' acceptable for the uncertain phīṭā hai?

5a: do you accept the conjectural division of leṅgūre as le + gure, 'taking from the guru' (supported only by the Tibetan blangs and Munidatta's mention of the guru's feet), or should the line fall back to 'taking it, know it plainly' with the guru left to a note? Is jāṇī better as the imperative 'know' (drafted, after the Tibetan comment) or 'having known'?
5a: the pack's glossary entry for p-dharma lists no variants; I used 'Dhāma' in the signature line as the variant I was told the entry carries. Please confirm it is recorded in the glossary.
Proposals: I proposed 'channel of excrement' and 'channel of urine' to sit beside the existing 'channel of semen' for Munidatta's reading of couplet 4. Useful now, or leave them for the weave?
